title: Thermodynamics: energy, work and gas processes
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 8

chapters.title: Choose the system and define the signs
chapters.formula: Delta U = Q - Wby; Q into system positive; expansion work positive
points: The zeroth law makes temperature comparison consistent.
Internal energy is a state function; heat and work describe transfers.
Absorbing 600 J while doing 250 J of work increases internal energy by 350 J.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. A gas warms up, pushes a piston, and lifts a weight. Where does the supplied energy go? Thermodynamics keeps that energy account. First choose the system: today it is the gas. Everything else is its surroundings. Thermal equilibrium means there is no net heat transfer between bodies in thermal contact. The zeroth law says that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. That is why a thermometer can compare temperatures consistently. Now choose signs. We'll call heat entering the gas positive, and work done by the gas on its surroundings positive. The first law then says the change in internal energy equals heat received minus work done by the gas. If it absorbs six hundred joules and does two hundred and fifty joules of work, its internal energy rises by three hundred and fifty joules. If instead the surroundings compress it and do work on it, our work by the gas is negative. Internal energy depends on the state. Heat and work depend on the process, so we don't say a gas contains a certain amount of heat. Some chemistry books use work on the system as positive and write a plus sign. Both conventions work, but never mix them in one solution.

chapters.title: Pressure-volume graphs measure work
chapters.formula: Wby = integral Pexternal dV; for quasistatic mechanical equilibrium use gas pressure
points: Expansion has positive work; compression has negative work.
A constant-pressure expansion at 2 x 10^5 Pa from 1 to 3 litres does 400 J.
Over a closed cycle Delta U = 0, so net heat equals net work.
chapters.script: Let's see where gas work comes from. Pressure pushes the piston with force pressure times area. A small piston movement changes the volume by area times displacement. Multiply them and the work element is external pressure times volume change. In a slow process close to mechanical equilibrium, the gas pressure tracks the resisting pressure, and the area under the pressure volume curve gives the work. For a constant pressure of two times ten to the power five pascals, let volume increase from one litre to three litres. The change is two litres, or zero point zero zero two cubic metres. Pressure times this change gives four hundred joules. During compression the volume change is negative, so work by the gas is negative. Don't forget that one litre is ten to the power minus three cubic metres. In a complete cycle, the gas returns to its initial state, and its internal energy change is zero. Therefore net heat received equals net work done. On a pressure volume graph, a clockwise loop gives positive net work; an anticlockwise loop gives negative net work. Different paths between the same endpoints can have different areas and therefore different work, while the internal energy change between those states remains the same. For a strongly irreversible process, don't substitute an undefined intermediate gas pressure into that integral.

chapters.title: Constant volume, constant pressure and constant temperature
chapters.formula: Isochoric: W = 0; isobaric: W = P Delta V; ideal-gas isothermal: Delta U = 0
points: At fixed volume, heat supplied changes internal energy when no other work occurs.
At fixed pressure an expanding gas can both warm and do work.
Reversible isothermal ideal-gas expansion gives W = n R T ln(Vf/Vi).
chapters.script: Process names are useful only if we understand what stays fixed. Isochoric means constant volume. With only pressure volume work allowed, a fixed volume means zero work, and heat supplied equals the internal energy increase. Isobaric means constant pressure. If the gas expands, some incoming energy does work and the rest changes internal energy. Isothermal means constant temperature, not zero heat transfer. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. So an isothermal ideal gas has zero internal energy change, and the first law gives heat received equal to work done. During a reversible isothermal expansion, pressure equals n R T divided by volume. Integrating gives work equal to n R T times the natural logarithm of the final to initial volume ratio. Suppose a problem gives n R T as one thousand joules and the gas doubles its volume. Multiply one thousand by the natural logarithm of two, about zero point six nine three. Work is approximately six hundred and ninety three joules, and the gas receives the same heat. If no heat entered, that ideal gas could not stay at the same temperature while doing positive work. Remember the ideal gas restriction: constant temperature does not automatically imply constant internal energy for every real substance.

chapters.title: Adiabatic does not mean constant temperature
chapters.formula: Q = 0; Delta U = -Wby; reversible ideal gas: P V^gamma = constant
points: Adiabatic means no heat crosses the boundary.
Expansion can cool the gas by reducing its internal energy.
For reversible adiabatic expansion, T V^(gamma - 1) is constant; these relations do not apply to every irreversible adiabatic process.
chapters.script: Now insulate the gas so that no heat crosses its boundary. That is an adiabatic process. If it expands and does work, the energy must come from its internal energy. For an ideal gas that usually means its temperature falls. Let's contrast this with isothermal expansion. Isothermal expansion stays at constant temperature because suitable heat exchange replaces the energy used for work. Adiabatic expansion has no such replacement. In a reversible adiabatic ideal gas process with constant heat capacities, pressure times volume to the power gamma is constant. Gamma is the ratio of molar heat capacity at constant pressure to that at constant volume. Combining this relation with the gas equation gives temperature times volume to the power gamma minus one constant. Try a gas with gamma five thirds and initial temperature four hundred kelvin. It expands reversibly and adiabatically to eight times its initial volume. The temperature ratio is one over eight raised to the two thirds power. Eight to the two thirds is four, so the final temperature is one hundred kelvin in this idealized model. But do not apply this reversible relation blindly. An ideal gas freely expanding into a vacuum in an isolated container does no external work and receives no heat. Its internal energy, and hence its temperature, stays unchanged. Adiabatic alone is not enough to choose the power law.

chapters.title: The second law adds direction
chapters.formula: Cyclic engine: Wnet = Qhot - Qcold; efficiency = Wnet/Qhot
points: A cyclic engine cannot convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work.
Heat does not move from cold to hot as the sole spontaneous effect.
An engine receiving 1000 J and rejecting 700 J delivers 300 J at 30 percent efficiency.
chapters.script: Energy conservation is necessary, but it doesn't tell us which processes can actually happen. The second law adds that direction. Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a cooler one, not the reverse as the only effect. A refrigerator can move heat from cold to hot, but it needs work input. Another statement says a cyclic engine cannot take heat from just one reservoir and turn all of it into work with no other effect. Our simple engine receives one thousand joules from a hot reservoir and rejects seven hundred joules to a colder reservoir each cycle. It delivers three hundred joules of net work. Divide that work by the heat received: efficiency is zero point three, or thirty percent. This is not the assertion that heat can never be completely converted to work in a single noncyclic process. The cycle and single reservoir conditions matter. A reversible process is an ideal limit that can be reversed while restoring both system and surroundings, with no net changes left behind. Friction, free expansion and heat flow across a finite temperature difference are irreversible. Moving slowly is not enough if friction is still present. For JEE problems, begin with the energy balance, name the process, check its assumptions and only then choose a special formula. That's the foundation for thermodynamic reasoning.

quiz.question: A gas absorbs 600 J and does 250 J work. Using Delta U = Q - Wby, Delta U is:
quiz.explanation: Heat in is positive, and work by is positive: Delta U = 600 - 250 = 350 J.

quiz.question: A quasistatic constant-pressure gas expansion at 2 x 10^5 Pa increases volume from 1 to 3 litres. Work by the gas is:
quiz.explanation: Delta V = 2 x 10^-3 m cubed. W = P Delta V = 400 J.

quiz.question: A reversible isothermal ideal-gas expansion doubles volume with nRT = 1000 J. Work is approximately:
quiz.explanation: W = nRT ln(2) = 1000 x 0.6931 = 693.1 J. Delta U = 0, so Q = W.

quiz.question: An ideal gas has gamma = 5/3 and starts at 400 K. In a reversible adiabatic process its volume becomes eight times larger. Final temperature is:
quiz.explanation: Tf = 400 x (1/8)^(2/3) = 400/4 = 100 K within the stated ideal-gas constant-capacity model.
